The Maṇḍala Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣad. "That is full"—thus [ends] the Peace Chant.
The First Brāhmaṇa.
The desire to know the reality of the Self:
The great sage Yājñavalkya indeed went to the world of Āditya. Having bowed to that Āditya, he said: "O Blessed One, please explain the reality of the Self of Āditya. || 1 ||
We worship Rāmacandra, whose manifestation is the inner and outer void in the form of the star, whose body is the fivefold ether, and who is perfectly realized through Rājayoga alone.
Now, indeed, this Maṇḍala Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣad, which is a division of the Śukla Yajurveda,
reveals the essence of Rājayoga— the illuminator of the three targets, the five voids, the two stars, and so forth— preceded by the disclosure of the subtle eight-limbed yoga (aṣṭāṅga-yoga).
It unfolds, illuminating [the truth]. A commentary on this work is now begun from its very small text.
This narrative, consisting of questions and answers between Yājñavalkya and Āditya, is intended for the purpose of praising the knowledge (*vidyā*).
He introduces the narrative with the words: "Yājñavalkya" (1).
The Promise of the Subtle Eightfold Yoga:
Nārāyaṇa said this: "Yoga consisting of the eight limbs, beginning with *yama* and accompanied by knowledge, is thus described.
(2.274) Having been questioned in this way by Yājñavalkya, he accepted that question and spoke.

The meaning is that He, who resides within the solar orb and is the ultimate refuge of all the worlds, spoke the answer to Yājñavalkya’s question. When the inquiry arises as to what that was, [the author] first describes the eight-limbed yoga beginning with *yama*, which serves as the means for realizing the true nature of the Self (*ātmatattva*) as asked; thus he says: "Knowledge," etc.
"Brahman alone is everything; there is nothing whatsoever apart from Brahman"—this knowledge is the goal (upeya); "accompanied by that" means having that [knowledge] as its core. || 2 ||
The fourfold restraint consists of victory over cold, heat, hunger, and sleep; constant tranquility, immovability, and the subduing of the senses from their objects—these are the *yamas*. (3)
Regarding the eight limbs, he describes the characteristic of the fourfold division of the pairs with the word "śītā" (cold, etc.).

Through the abandonment of the conceit of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and so forth, there occurs the cessation of [reactions] such as cold. Through the knowledge that "this object which has not been attained is not [mine]," there is constant peace.

The immobility of the mind toward its own desired object; the contemplation of reality regarding the senses and the objects of the senses constitutes the restraint of the senses and their objects. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of conjunction. The meaning is that these are the fourfold *yamās*. || 3 ||
The ninefold discipline consists of devotion to the guru, attachment to the path of truth, experiencing things as they come,
contentment through that experience of things, detachment, dwelling in solitude, and the cessation of mental activity.
The absence of desire for fruits and the state of dispassion are the observances (niyamas). || 4 ||

The ninefold classification of the rules is stated as follows: "Guru," etc. Constant worship of the Guru, who liberates one from one's own ignorance, without deceit is "devotion to the Guru" (*gurubhakti*); for the Śruti says, "One should always practice devotion to the Guru for the sake of the highest good. "Truth" (*satya*) is Brahman; the path that leads to its attainment and the realization thereof [is the next rule].

In this context, "attachment" (anurakti) means clinging. It is the experience of the reality of Brahman, which arises through the grace of the scriptures and the teacher by virtue of its nature as unsurpassed bliss.
Contentment (tuṣṭi), moreover, comes solely from the experience of that reality, and not from the experience of external objects. Even when there is contentment—

Non-attachment (*niḥsaṅgatā*). Dwelling in solitude at all three times—beginning, middle, and end—is as follows: the initial solitude is the deliberate restraint of the mind in a secluded place; the intermediate solitude is the deliberate restraint of the mind in a secluded place or even among people; [the final solitude is] in a secluded place... (p. 275)

In a place with people, the effortless restraint of the mind is internal solitude; the meaning is that whoever has achieved solitude by whatever means, at whatever time, should dwell right there. The cessation of the mind is the firm conviction that the mind does not exist apart from oneself.

Non-attachment to the fruits of actions performed by oneself; the absence of desire for all objects other than the Self, viewing them as if they were vomit, urine, or excrement; and the state of universal dispassion. The two words "and" (ca) are used everywhere to signify conjunction. These observances (niyamas) are of nine kinds. || 4 ||
The exposition of the six ancillaries beginning with posture:
the practice of a comfortable seat and dwelling there for a long time—such is the rule regarding posture. || 5 ||

Prāṇāyāma consists of inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka) in the sequence of sixteen, sixty-four, and thirty-two counts respectively. (6) Pratyāhāra is the withdrawal of the mind from the objects of the senses, that is, from sense-objects. (7) [This occurs] in consciousness preceded by the turning away from sense-objects.

The stabilization of the mind is retention (dhāraṇā). || 8 || The one-pointed concentration of consciousness upon the entire body is meditation (dhyāna). || 9 || The forgetting of meditation is absorption (samādhi). || 10 ||

The rule for posture (*āsana*) is stated: "That which is comfortable" (*sukha*). That state in which a mental modification (*vṛtti*) of an unbroken form arises with ease is the "comfortable posture-modification" (*sukhāsana-vṛtti*). That in which one dwells for a long time without effort is "long-term dwelling in the posture" (*cirāsana-vāsa*). (5) He states the definition of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*): "Inhalation" (*pūraka*), etc.

The meaning is that *pūraka* (inhalation) is measured by a duration of sixteen *mātrās*, *kumbhaka* (retention) is four times that, and *recaka* (exhalation) is half of that. [Verse 6] He states the definition of *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal of the senses): "From the objects... [Verse 7]
He states the characteristics of *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi*: "In all cases, regarding the object... (verse 8).

The meaning is that just as the space delimited by various jars, bowls, and so forth remains one even when they are broken, so it is here. (9) Samādhi refers to nirvikalpa-samādhi (non-conceptual absorption), because it swallows up the threefold division [of subject, object, and act of knowing]. (10)
Thus are the subtle limbs, which are the fruit of the knowledge of the eight limbs of subtle yoga. He who knows this becomes a partaker of liberation. || 11 ||

Thus, he states the fruit of the knowledge of the eight-limbed yoga with the word "evam" (thus). The subtle eight limbs—by means of his own internal knowledge in accordance with them—he becomes a partaker of liberation. || 11 ||
Thus ends the first section:
The Elimination of the Five Faults of the Body.
There are five faults of the body: desire, anger, sighing, fear, and sleep. (1)
The remedy for that, however, consists of freedom from volitional constructs, patience, moderation in diet, serenity, and devotion to the reality of the self. (2)

Raising the objection as to how that which is delimited by a body—possessing the five defects—can be a partaker of liberation, he says "of the body" (*dehasya*), stating that its attainment is possible because there exists a means for its removal. To the question "What are those [defects]?", he replies "desire" (*kāma*) and so forth. The sequential removal of them is as follows: through the absence of volitional construction (*niḥsaṅkalpataḥ*), there is the cessation of desire and the rest.

From forbearance comes the cessation of anger; from breath-control characterized by moderate diet comes steadiness of breath; from the abandonment of the notion of duality everywhere comes the cessation of fear;
and from the cultivation of the reality of the supreme truth comes the cessation of the sleep of one's own ignorance. Thus...
The meaning is that through the pacification of the five defects, one becomes a partaker of liberation. || 2 ||

Relying upon the subtle path to cross the ocean of worldly existence— which has the stars for its appearance, the fruit of that [existence] as its nature, sleep and fear as its serpents, violence and the like as its waves, craving as its whirlpools, and wives as its mud— one must proceed.

One should behold the Savior (Tāraka), transcending the qualities such as sattva and the rest. Between the eyebrows is the Savior-Brahman, whose form is a mass of the splendor of Being-Consciousness-Bliss.

Fearing that there might be no means for sentient beings to cross the shoreless ocean of saṃsāra, he states that by relying on the boat of the *tāraka* (the Savior) which has the three targets as its domain, that ocean can indeed be crossed: [The verse: "Obeisance to you, O Blessed One, who have become the Savior (*tāraka*) for the world; For those sinking in the great ocean of existence, Which is difficult to cross and devoid of refuge. p. 277) [The word] "sleep" (nidrā) [is used]. Regarding how the ocean-nature of saṃsāra is established, [the text says] "sleep," and so forth.

In order to cross—that is, to traverse—the ocean of saṃsāra characterized by the aforementioned attributes, there is the subtle path that will be described hereafter. || 3 || Regarding what that "deliverer" (tāraka) is, [the text says] "between the eyebrows" (bhrūmadhya).

For one who gazes at the tip of the nose, a light is seen between the eyebrows; this is because *saccidānanda* (Being-Consciousness-Bliss), being all-pervasive, is present even within the form of the mass of light conceptualized by the eyes and the mind.
Since the form of the mass of light consisting of *saccidānanda* that shines between the eyebrows is the very nature of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), [it is perceived there].

Because it carries across the ocean of saṃsāra—characterized by the existence of things other than itself—to the multitude of devotees who take refuge in it, it possesses the quality of being a "savior" (tāraka).
In reality, because it expands [all] as its own sole essence, it is designated as the "Savior-Brahman" (Tāraka-Brahman). || 4 ||
The attainment of the Star (Tāraka) occurs through the observation of the three targets; the means for attaining that [Star] is the observation of those three targets. || 5 ||
In response to the inquiry, "What is the means for that?", he says: "The means for its attainment. The meaning is: "Know [this].
The vision of the internal target is the Suṣumnā, which has the luster of the sun, extending from the Mūlādhāra to the Brahma-randhra.
In the midst of that is Kuṇḍalinī, equal to ten million flashes of lightning and as subtle as a lotus fiber;
therein occurs the cessation of darkness. From the vision of her, there is the cessation of all sins. || 6 ||

When the two ear-cavities are opened by the tips of the index fingers, a sound like a hissing *phut* arises; when the mind is fixed there, one perceives a blue light in the center of the eyes. It is the same in the heart as well. || 7 ||

Regarding the question "What are the three targets?", they are of three kinds according to the division of internal, external, and intermediate. Among these, he states the definition of the internal target and its fruit, beginning with the word "mūla" (the root): the Suṣumnā nerve exists resting upon the neck of the lute (vīṇādaṇḍa). Therein resides the Kuṇḍalinī power, possessing a brilliance equal to ten million flashes of lightning. There, within the mind...

When [the mind] has become steady, there is the cessation of the darkness of one's own ignorance. By beholding that space which exists within the *kuṇḍalinī*, the cessation of all sins occurs. (p. 278) Inserting both index fingers between the two ears is the *mukunda-mudrā*.

"By that, [it is called] *tarjanī*. Because the two index fingers (*tarjanī*) cover the two ears, the sound of a hissing breath (*phūtkāra*) and so forth arises therein. When the mind is fixed there, the practitioner sees "the eye," and so forth.
It is not only in the sound (*nāda*), but he likewise sees thus within the heart as well. || 7 ||
Regarding the observation of external objects (*bahir-lakṣya-darśana*),

the external object consists of [visualizations] at the tip of the nose, respectively endowed with two colors— blue luster, dark green, red resembling a wave, and shimmering yellow— at distances of four, six, eight, ten, and twelve finger-breadths.
That yogi perceives the nature of space (vyomatva). For the person who gazes at the portion of space with a moving gaze, rays of light appear before his vision; his gaze then becomes steady.
When one perceives the light measuring twelve finger-breadths above the head, then one attains immortality. || 10 ||

Having stated the extent of the internal object (*antarlakṣya*), he proceeds to describe the extent of the external object (*bahirlakṣya*) with the word "externally" (*bahiḥ*). Having made his two eyes even, the yogi, according to the degree of his own practice,
gradually [perceives] the state of space (*vyomatva*), the nature of the void, at a distance of four fingers up to twelve fingers from the tip of his own nose.
He sees it. Of what kind is the sky? Here, it possesses a visible blue luster;

it resembles the quality of slight darkness and, at first glance, has a reddish appearance, yet it is distinguished by a shimmering yellow color. Among these, the colors blue and yellow are predominant.
The dark and other colors, however, are subordinate. Thus, the meaning is that the sky is characterized by two colors. When one perceives it in this way, then one becomes a yogin. || 8 ||
He says that by seeing in this way, the vision supported by the mind becomes steady—"calet" (it moves).
"Svadṛśyagre" means before one's own object of sight. "Mayūkhāḥ" means rays. "Uddṛṣṭiḥ" is the gaze directed toward that [object], the vision fixed upon it.
|| 9 || He says that seeing the light above the head results in the fruit of immortality—"śīrṣe" (at the head). When...
This yogi is above his own head. || 10 ||
The vision of the central object:
the central object is like the various colors in a painting at dawn, or like the rows of flames from the sun, moon, and fire, yet devoid of them— like the intermediate space.
He sees. || 11 || He becomes one who takes on that form. || 12 ||
Through practice, it becomes the unchanging space devoid of qualities (*guṇarahitākāśa*).
It becomes the supreme space (*parākāśa*), resembling dense darkness with the form of shimmering stars.
It becomes the great space (*mahākāśa*), shining like the fire of cosmic destruction (*kālānala*).
The space of reality (*tattvākāśa*) becomes brilliantly radiant as the most excellent, supreme, and non-dual;
the solar space (*sūryākāśa*) becomes like the brilliance of ten million suns. || 13 ||
Thus, through practice, one becomes identical with that, he who knows this. 14.

Having described the internal and external characteristics, he reveals the characteristic of the intermediate object of focus with the words "madhya" (intermediate), etc.: "In the morning," and so forth, [the yogi] [fixes his gaze] in the space before him at a distance that is not too far. || 11 ||

Anticipating the question, "What would result from such a vision?", he says, "In that form" (tadākāra), [implying] that by seeing the fivefold space (*vyomapañcaka*), one becomes identical with it and even attains its state.
He states the fruit of knowledge through practice with the word "thus" (evam). 12–14.
Thus ends the second section:
Yoga is twofold, distinguished by the Tāraka and Manasaka types;
know that this yoga is also twofold according to the preceding and subsequent methods.
One should know that the former is the Tāraka [vidyā], and the latter is the Amanaska.

The *tāraka* is of two kinds: the embodied (*mūrti*) *tāraka* and the formless (*amūrta*) *tāraka*. That which ends at the senses is the embodied *tāraka*; that which transcends the pair of eyebrows is the formless *tāraka*. (1)
Regarding the question of what would result from the practice of the five voids (*vyomapañcaka*), he says "that" (*tat*) to indicate that at the culmination of this practice,
the perfection of the mind through the Star (*tārakamanaskasiddhi*) is attained. Thus, he refers to that yoga which was previously described as the practice of the five voids.
Regarding the question, "What is the Tāraka with form (mūrtitāraka), and what is the Tāraka without form (amūrtitāraka)?"—

it is stated [in the verse beginning with] "That which... (verse 1) that from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *ājñācakra* is the Tāraka with form, and from the *ājñācakra* up to the *sahasrāra* is the Tāraka without form.
Regarding the method of mental application:
one should practice both while joined with the mind.
The internal vision joined with the mind leads to the light of the Tāraka. || 2 ||
Raising the objection that the perception of the object depends upon the eyes, so what is the use of the mind?

[The author] replies with the word "mind" (manaḥ): it is one whose vision is assisted by the mind who, having become inward-sighted, becomes a grasper of the Tāraka, and not one whose vision is merely external. || 2 ||
The appearance of light within the cavity between the pair of eyebrows is the "first star. This is the first star. || 3 ||
He describes the nature of the previous *tāraka* [mantra] as follows: "The pair of eyebrows... (verse 3).
The northern star is the supreme state beyond the mind. A great light exists in the upper portion of the root of the palate;
from the vision of that, the supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā* are attained. || 4 ||
He states the nature of the subsequent [stage] along with its fruit: "But the subsequent... [and so on]. Accomplishment (siddhi) occurs. || 4 ||
The culmination of the *uttaratāraka* is the *śāmbhavī*;

this *śāmbhavī-mudrā* occurs when the gaze—both internal and external—is fixed upon the object of perception and is devoid of blinking or opening. In all tantras, it is the secret Great Knowledge (*mahāvidyā*).
Through knowledge of that, there is the cessation of saṃsāra; its worship bestows the fruit of liberation.

(281) He states that the Śāmbhavī Mudrā alone, culminating in the upward star (the point between the eyebrows), bestows the fruit of liberation—namely, "the object of focus" (lakṣya). And so says another Vedic scripture:
"The inner object of focus, with the gaze directed outward, free from closing and opening the eyes."
This is that Śāmbhavī Mudrā, concealed in all the tantras.
Thus [it is said]. Knowledge of Śāmbhavī brings about the cessation of saṃsāra; he states that the worship of her yogis yields the fruit of liberation: "That" (tad), etc. (verse 5).
The characteristic of the internal target is that the internal target is of the nature of water and light, to be known by the great sages,
and invisible to both internal and external senses.

Furthermore, regarding what is meant by "the internal object" (*antarlakṣya*), he states that it is precisely that which is beyond the range of the entire collection of sense organs; thus he says: "Internal" (*antar*) || 6 ||
Thus ends the third section:
the disagreement among disputants regarding the internal object of focus.
The internal object of focus is the water-light within the thousand-petaled lotus (sahasrāra) in the cave of the intellect (buddhiguhā).
Others say that the internal object of focus (*antarlakṣya*) is a human form beautiful in all its limbs.
Some maintain that the internal object of focus is the tranquil, blue-throated Lord Umā’s consort, five-faced and situated within the circle inside the head. [He is] the size of a thumb.
Some say that the inner target is the Puruṣa. || 1 ||

(p. 282) Regarding the object of the internal target (*antarlakṣya*), he states—through the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthadṛṣṭi*)—the unity of the target which is the domain of all disputants' conceptual constructions, and how, by seeing that [target], one reaches the state of being established in Brahman, with the words "sahasrāra" and so forth. Within the cave of the intellect (*buddhiguhā*), there are yogins; others are Vaiṣṇavas; some...
The Śaivas; some are worshippers of the Dahara-vidyā. || 1 ||
The method for perceiving the Self as pervading all objects of perception is this:

all that has been described through conceptual distinctions is indeed the Self alone. He who perceives that object of perception through the vision of the pure Self becomes one who is firmly established in Brahman. || 2 ||

It is said by Yogīs and others from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Thus, he says "that object" (verse 2) to describe one who is established in Brahman and perceives the unity of the internal object.
For one established in the Self, there is the attainment of the state of Brahman:

the individual soul (*jīva*), the twenty-fifth principle, having abandoned the twenty-four principles imagined by itself, becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) through the firm conviction, "I am the twenty-sixth, the Supreme Self. || 3 ||
Thus, by perceiving the internal target, having himself become the internal target during the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti), he becomes the unbroken orb of the supreme space. || 4 ||

He states that the individual soul (jīva), established in its own true nature, becomes liberated by abandoning the principles lower than itself through the knowledge of the principles higher than itself—thus he says: "The soul.
[These consist of] the twenty: the five organs of knowledge, the five organs of action, the five senses, the five vital breaths, and the five elements.

The four internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) constitute the twenty-four principles (tattvas). The individual soul (jīva), conditioned by these, is the twenty-fifth, according to the Vedic scripture which states, "the self becomes the twenty-fifth.
That which is free from the connection with all such limiting adjuncts (upādhi) is the twenty-sixth; this is the meaning. [3] [He is] liberated while living (jīvanmukta).

Anticipating the question of what state one attains, he says "evam" (thus), meaning that immediately upon the abandonment of the identification with the body while still alive, one becomes Brahman itself;
the sense is that one becomes the Supreme Self. || 4 ||
Thus ends the fourth section;
thus ends the first Brāhmaṇa;
[now begins] the second Brāhmaṇa.
Then Yājñavalkya questioned the Puruṣa of the solar orb regarding the state of being the inner object of focus for the Self that is the light of all supports:
"O Blessed One, the nature of the inner object of focus and so forth has been described in many ways; yet I have not understood it. Please explain that."

To me [he spoke]. He said: "The cause of the five elements, resembling a mass of lightning, likewise possesses four seats; in its center, the manifestation of reality occurs. It is extremely hidden and unmanifest. || 2 ||

Although Yājñavalkya already knew [the answer], he asks again about the measure of the internal object (*antarlakṣya*) for the sake of facilitating the comprehension of those of dull intellect; thus he says: "Now" (*atha*). Why? He asks: "O Venerable One" (*bhagavan*). [The answer is: "As it truly is by me" (*yathāvad mayā*). To that question, the Venerable One gave the reply. What was it? "Five" (*pañca*).

Because it is the cause of the five elements for the Self whose internal object of focus is itself, according to the Vedic scripture: "From the Self, space was produced. It has the appearance of a mass of lightning because its form is a mass of light. Like that light, in accordance with the perspectives of those beginning with one's own ignorance, it exists in the state of equilibrium of the qualities of *tamas*, *rajas*, and *sattva*.
That which possesses four seats (pīṭhas) by way of the division of the four states beginning with waking,

or by way of the division of the four parts beginning with the gross (sthūla) within the sphere of one's own ignorance (svāvidyāpada)— that is "four-seated" (catuṣpīṭha); for waking and the other states serve as the seats (āsanas) of Viśva, Virāṭ, Otrā, and so forth.
He says "that" (tat) to show that he himself is the illuminator of the stage of ignorance (*avidyāpāda*) which is well-established:

"In the midst of that stage of ignorance, having swallowed the entire collection of its specific qualities, the light of the Fourth-of-the-Fourth (*turyaturya-jyotiḥ*), which is the manifestation of reality, exists eternally. To the question, "If such a light exists, why is it not perceived? [the text continues:]
He said: "He"—to one whose vision is veiled by his own covering, he remains exceedingly hidden and unmanifest. (2)
The fruit of the knowledge of the self is light;
it is to be known by one who has boarded the boat of that knowledge. Its objective is both external and internal. (3)
Within that, the universe is dissolved; it is the unbroken circle transcending sound, the point, and the digit;
its nature is both with attributes and without attributes. He who knows that is liberated. 4.
(284) By what means can that be known? To this he says: "That.

Having crossed the ocean of one's own ignorance by boarding the boat of knowledge, that which is its further shore should be known as "Self alone" (*svamātra*). As to what that is like, he says: "That is the objective (*lakṣya*) both external and internal."

Because it is characterized as the locus for the superimposition and negation of external and internal mental constructs (kalpanā). For this very reason, [the mantra] is dissolved within that [center], because it is the support of dissolution (layādhāra). One might object that being the support of dissolution would imply the presence of attributes (saviśeṣatā);
therefore, he says: "That," meaning that which is the locus of all, is the *nāda*.

The meaning is that it is the non-dual, partless, single-flavored pure consciousness (cinmātra), established through the negation of specific attributes such as sound (nāda) and so forth, and is devoid of any counter-correlate (niṣpratiyogika).

To the objection that it might possess attributes and be distinct from that [pure consciousness], he says: "saguṇa" (with attributes). This refers to the state of being either a specific attribute or a non-specific attribute belonging to that [consciousness].
"It is established in the vision of one's own ignorance and so forth, not established in itself. He states the fruit of this knowledge: "He who knows that" (verse 4).
Through the Śāmbhavī mudrā, there is the realization of that [state]:
first, the circle of fire; above that, the circle of the sun;
in its center, the nectar-filled circle of the moon; and in the center of that, the circle of the indivisible splendor of Brahman.
That which is as brilliantly white as a streak of lightning is indeed the characteristic of Śāmbhavī. || 5 ||
He states the means for attaining that by knowing which one becomes liberated, beginning with the words "In the beginning":

having ascended to the Siddhāsana, for the yogi practicing the Ṣaṇmukhī Mudrā, the circle of fire (vahnimaṇḍala) and so forth are perceived in sequence; at the conclusion, that very state is the Śāmbhavī, which generates the condition of Unmanī.
The meaning is that it comes into being. || 5 ||
The procedure for the vision of the full moon:

upon seeing it, there are three visions—namely, the new moon, the first day [of the lunar fortnight], and the full moon. The vision with eyes closed is the new moon vision; half-opened [eyes] is the first-day vision; and fully opened [eyes] is...
It becomes full. Among those [states], the practice of the full moon must be performed. Its objective mark is the tip of the nose; then, at the root of the palate, an intense darkness is seen.
Through that practice, a light in the form of an unbroken orb is seen. That indeed is Existence-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda).
He becomes Brahman. || 7 ||

(p. 285) He states the means for seeing that [reality] with the words "taddarśane" (in the seeing of that). To the question, "How is there a threefold nature of vision? he replies, "amā" (the new moon). Regarding the phrase "there, with eyes closed," etc. (6), to the question, "What is the object characterized by these three visions? he replies, "tallakṣyam" (that which is characterized by them). To the question, "What is seen by looking at the tip of the nose? he replies, "tadā" (then). Thus...

Through the practice of that, by the vision of that, it is that very thing; because that which is other than Brahman—being existence-consciousness-bliss—is sought after, the meaning is that it is indeed that very form of innate bliss. || 7 ||
The culmination of the vision of the full moon is indeed the Śāmbhavī state.
Thus, when the mind dissolves into innate bliss (sahajānanda), then the Śāmbhavī arises;
they call that very state Khecarī. || 8 ||

Regarding this, he states that the dissolution of the mind itself is the Śāmbhavī state with the words "evam" (thus). This is because, in the final consummation, the Śāmbhavī and Khecarī states reach completion within a single focal point. || 8 ||
The accomplishment of the mudrās and their signs;
through the practice of those, stability of mind; from that, stability of intellect. (9) Those signs:
at first it is seen like a star; then like a diamond mirror; after that—
First, the orb of the full moon; then, the orb of jewel-light; then, the orb of the midday sun; and then, the orb of the crest of fire is seen in succession.

To the question, "What would result from the practice of mudrā? he says: "That" (verse 9). "Its signs" means the signs of its accomplishment. To the question, "Which ones? he says: "At first," etc. "Like a star" means like a constellation;
"like a polished vajra" and "like a mirror" is the meaning. And thus says the Śruti:
Frost, smoke, sun, fire, wind, fireflies, lightning, crystal, and the moon—
these are the preliminary forms that bring about the manifestation of Brahman in yoga.
Thus [ends the tenth].
Thus ends the first section:
the experience of the direct manifestation of the nature of the *praṇava*, and its signs.
At that time, there is a westward-facing radiance consisting of crystal, smoky, bindu, nāda, kalā—
The radiance of the stars, fireflies, lamps, eyes, gold, the nine precious gems, and so forth is seen; that very [radiance] is the form of the *praṇava*. || 1 ||
When these signs are thus seen, then there occurs the experience of the inwardly directed light.

To the question of what signs are seen therein, [the text says]: "Like a crystal," and so forth. These are seen by one who practices the contemplation of the *praṇava*. By the word "bindu" (point), the principle of the mind (*manas-tattva*) is meant.
By the word *nāda* is meant the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*), and by the word *kalā* is meant the principle of the Great One (*mahattattva*); the remainder is clear.
Having thus observed this, he says "that" (verse 1) to show that all of this is of the nature of the *praṇava*.
The attainment of the *praṇava* through the six-faced [mudrā] consists of unifying the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, performing the *ghṛta-kumbhaka* retention,
and forming the six-faced [mudrā] with the fingers of both hands through firm contemplation upon the tip of the nose.
Upon hearing the sound beginning with the syllable Om, the mind becomes absorbed therein. || 2 ||

He states that Brahman, which is the meaning of the *praṇava*, is the locus for the dissolution of the mind and its effects, preceded by the sixfold means—beginning with *prāṇa*—according to the method of *haṭhayoga*. Thus he says "prāṇa" etc.:
the yogi who has maintained the *kumbhaka* [breath-retention] therein, at the conclusion of the *nāda* within Brahman. (2)
For one who knows the *praṇava*, there is no attachment to action;
for him, there is no taint of action. Indeed, it is said that action must be performed during the rising and setting of the sun;
but for one who knows thus, because there is neither rising nor setting for the sun of consciousness (*cid-āditya*), there is an absence of all action. || 3 ||
p. 287) For one whose mind is dissolved in Brahman, there is no stain of action, because the yogin is untainted.
Anticipating the objection as to how there can be such untaintedness when duties remain to be performed, [the text explains that] actions are merely instrumental to the rising and setting of the sun.

He states that even the assertion that "this [Self] is untainted because there is an absence of rising and setting for the sun-like qualified Self, and consequently an absence of action caused by them" is merely figurative: "By action a living being is bound; through knowledge one attains immortality. Therefore, ascetics who see the further shore do not perform ritual actions.
Thus, according to the sacred scripture. || 3 ||
Through the state of *unmanī*, the accomplishment of the mindless (*amanaska*) occurs;
by dissolving sound and time, having transcended day and night, one attains identity with Brahman through all-pervading, perfect knowledge by means of the power of the *unmanī* state.
The state beyond mind becomes mindless. || 4 ||
To the question, "What would result from the dissolution of the resonance of the *praṇava* in this way?

he says, "By the [dissolution] of sound," etc., meaning that the oneness with Brahman, which is devoid of all mental constructs (*kalanā*), comes about through the dissolution of time and sound consisting of both the signifier and the signified. Here, "sound" refers to the manifold of signifiers (*abhidhāna-prapañca*).

Time consists of the conceptualization of objects of expression; for one with false vision (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the dissolution of those two is precisely the sublation of their existence through the knowledge of hearing. From that, realization arises. By means of the certain knowledge that there is no triad of states characterized by day and night apart from Brahman, one transcends it.

Then, having become [one with] the perfect right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) which is fulfilled by the impossibility of any generality (*sāmānya*) beyond Brahman, the state of *unmanī* arises. *Unmanī* is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).

By that, there is oneness with Brahman, wherein Brahman—established through the total negation (*sarvāpahnava*) of all else—is one's own self alone, free from all opposition (*niṣpratiyogika-svamātra*).

It comes to be so; for there is no oneness between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśa*) once they have attained a state of separation—this is the meaning. To the question, "What is born from *unmanī*? he says: "By *unmanī*. Since the scripture states, "That is the nature of the mindless (*amanaska*); therein is no stain of conceptualization," the very word *amanaska* refers to Brahman itself. || 4 ||
The method of worship without the mind (*amanaskapūjā*) is as follows: non-mentation is meditation (*dhyāna*); the relinquishing of all karmic activity is the invocation (*āvāhana*);
certain knowledge is the seat (*āsana*); the state of *unmanī* is the water for the feet (*pādya*); and perpetual non-mentation is the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*).

(288) Constant radiance is the bathing in the flow of boundless nectar (*amṛta*). Pervasive contemplation is the fragrance. Abiding in the nature of vision is the unbroken offering. Attainment of consciousness is the flower. The nature of the fire of consciousness is the incense. The nature of the sun of consciousness is the lamp. The unification with the nectar of the full moon is [the offering].

The food offering is stillness; circumambulation is the state of being unwavering; prostration is the realization "I am He"; praise is silence; and dismissal is universal contentment—he who knows thus. || 5 ||
Raising the doubt as to how there can be any figurative application of meditation (*dhyāna*) and the like toward that Brahman which is beyond the mind (*amanaska*), he says "of that" (*tasya*),

explaining that according to the Vedic injunction "one should worship with the sense of 'I am He' (*so'ham*)," the very contemplation "I am That" (*tadasmīti*) is itself its worship; for it is the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of an undivided whole (*akhaṇḍākāra*) directed toward the effulgent Brahman.

The meaning is "bathing. In all cases, there is the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) that [everything] is Brahman. The food offering (*naivedya*) consists of the nectar flowing from the full moon disc shimmering within the space between the eyebrows and the *sahasrāra*, which is unified and takes the form of an ocean of nectar. It is constant contentment. This is precisely it.
The meaning is that through the continuous contemplation of Brahman, one becomes Brahman itself. || 5 ||
Thus ends the second section:
the attainment of liberation through the contemplation of Brahman.
In this way, when the triad [of subject, object, and means] has been discarded, one becomes like a waveless ocean or a lamp situated in a windless place.
The light of absolute liberation (kaivalya-jyoti), which is free from existence and non-existence and devoid of the fluctuations of speech and thought, comes into being. || 1 ||

Having raised the doubt as to how a yogi attains the state of Brahman when the contemplation of Brahman is constrained by the threefold division [of knower, known, and knowing], it is explained that this occurs through right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), which consists of the contemplation that Brahman— established by the negation of everything— is one's own self alone, devoid of any counter-correlate (*niṣpratiyogika*).
He states "Thus" (evam) because the attainment of the state of Brahman is desired through the swallowing of the triad beginning with the meditator (dhyātṛ).

The meaning is that for the knower, only his own self alone remains as the light of absolute liberation (kaivalya-jyotis), which is established by the awakening to the impossibility of the conceptualization of existence and non-existence regarding anything other than himself—neither "it exists" nor "it does not exist. || 1 ||
The true nature of the knower of Brahman:
by means of thorough knowledge of the end of waking and sleep, one becomes a knower of Brahman. || 2 ||

Regarding the question, "How can he possess the status of Brahman without being a knower of Brahman?"—his status as Brahman is indeed established through the knowledge of the entirety of Brahman. He states that one may be a knower of Brahman through the knowledge of Brahman that is not complete: "jāgrad... (II.ii.1).
The distinction between deep sleep (suṣupti) and meditative absorption (samādhi):

although there is no difference between deep sleep and meditative absorption in terms of the dissolution of the mind, there is a great distinction between the two; for [in deep sleep] the mind is dissolved in darkness and thus lacks the quality of being a cause for liberation. In meditative absorption, however, the modifications of darkness have been attenuated.

The dissolution of the phenomenal world (prapañca) occurs within the witness-consciousness (sākṣicaitanya), which consists of an undivided mental modification (akhaṇḍākāravṛtti) conditioned by that [Brahman’s] form; for the phenomenal world is imagined by the mind. || 4 ||

Since deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and meditative absorption (*samādhi*) are similar in that the mind is dissolved in both, one might think that both could be causes of either bondage or liberation; therefore, he says: "Deep sleep... [Verse 3]. Why is that? Because of the darkness (*tamas*). [Verse 3]. Why is that? Because of the world-appearance (*prapañca*). [Verse 4].
For the knower of Brahman, there is the state of Brahman;
because of the absence of any distinction from it, even when he has occasionally gone outside, there is only the appearance of falsity.
The knower of Brahman, whose sole sphere of experience is the realization of the eternally blissful and once-and-for-all manifest [Brahman], becomes that very thing. || 5 ||

Because the consciousness that is interwoven with each of those [mental states] is one when their respective effects are absent, therefore, even when the mind has gone outward, the illusory nature of the phenomenal world projected by it is perceived.
Thus, he says "sakṛt" (once) to show that the knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself in every respect.
"Always unobscured by the three veils beginning with ignorance, [he is] 'once-returning' and so forth. || 5 ||

(290) Liberation is accomplished through meditation on the Supreme Self preceded by the renunciation of volitional constructs (*saṃkalpa*). For one whose volitional constructs have been destroyed, liberation is held in the palm of the hand.
Therefore, having abandoned both existence and non-existence, one becomes liberated through meditation on the Supreme Self. (6)

Again and again, in all states, having abandoned the knower and the known, meditation and the object of meditation, the characterized and the uncharacterized, and the visible and the invisible, as well as reasoning and refutation, one becomes liberated while living—he who knows thus. || 7 ||

He says, "Of whom," [implying] that the existence and non-existence of mental constructs (*saṃkalpa*) would be the causes of bondage and liberation; therefore, from this very fact, the existence and non-existence of those constructs—namely, "it exists" or "it does not exist"—[are determined].
The supreme Self, which is without a counter-correlative, is one's own nature alone.

By means of meditation on the Supreme Self manifested through knowledge. (6) He states the fruit of such knowledge with the word "again" (*punaḥ*). Even when Brahman is known by the intellect that remains as one's own self (*svāvaśeṣadhiyā*), if an activity consisting of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and so forth should arise again by means of an intellect that perceives something other than oneself (*svātiriktadhiyā*), then [the phrase] "again and again" (*punaḥ-punaḥ*) applies. This is the locus for the abandonment of that [activity].
The meaning is that he who knows thus—"I am Brahman"—is a wise man who becomes liberated while living. || 7 ||
Thus ends the third section.
The five states, beginning with waking, are the five states: waking, dreaming, deep sleep, the fourth (turīya), and that which transcends the fourth (turīyātīta). || 1 ||
What is the cause of bondage and liberation? To this he says: "Five. What are they?—"Waking," etc. The meaning is: the five states. || 1 ||

The volition for worldly activity (*pravṛtti-saṃkalpa*) occurs when the individual soul (*jīva*), active in the waking state and attached to the path of worldly engagement, desires: "May there be no hell or other results of sin, and may there be heaven as the fruit of auspicious deeds. || 2 ||
In that context, he explains the intentions regarding the engagement and withdrawal of the living being (jīva) with the words "While waking," etc.
[Verse 2]: The fruit of heaven arises from auspicious karma. Desiring it in this way, the ignorant person becomes bound by saṃsāra. || 2 ||

His resolve is toward renunciation; thus, having embraced dispassion, he turns away from the cycle of worldly existence—the bondage of birth arising from the fruits of action—as being impure, and proceeds upon the path of withdrawal directed toward liberation. || 3 ||

While many remain in this state, someone—through the grace of the Lord, who is satisfied by the offering of the fruits of actions performed over the course of many millions of births—becomes engaged in the path of renunciation;
thus he says: "In this way," referring to one who is thus weary of such saṃsāra.
He comes into being; from this arises the birth of the fruit of karma. || 3 ||
That very path is the way to cross over saṃsāra; having relied upon a guru for the sake of crossing over saṃsāra, having abandoned desire and the like,
and performing prescribed duties, one who is endowed with the fourfold qualifications [should meditate] in the center of the heart-lotus.
Having attained the form that is to be perceived within the mere existence of the Blessed One,
and having obtained the memory of the bliss of Brahman released during the state of deep sleep, [one realizes]: "For a certain time, I alone was non-dual due to the activity of ignorance."
Having discarded the notion "I am Taijasa" as a fruitless result of forgotten impressions from the waking state, and having likewise ceased both of those [waking and dreaming], one realizes:
"Now I am the Prājña alone; though there are differences in states due to differences in locations, yet there is indeed nothing other than Me.
Thus, by discerning the nature of the Self, and casting out even the scent of duality with the realization "I am the pure non-dual Brahman," one attains liberation.

Having ascended the path to liberation, which is formed by the Supreme Brahman—shaped into that very form through meditation on the solar disc manifested within one's own heart—he becomes fully matured. || 4 ||

Having abandoned the outward-oriented activity of desire and so forth for some time previously during one’s own state of ignorance; having attained the state of the Taijasa by swallowing the objective world of the Viśva, thinking "I am the Taijasa";
and through the exhaustion of that enjoyment, that which is accompanied by the mental constructs of waking and dreaming is called "both" (tadubhaya).

Because of the dissolution through self-knowledge of the distinctions of states—such as waking and so forth—which are imagined by one’s own ignorance due to the differences in those states, that which remains is the Supreme Brahman. "Indeed, there is nothing other than Me"—this is the discrimination regarding birth (*jāti-viveka*). Birth (*jāti*) refers to that which is born as something distinct from Brahman; [it is understood that] birth and so forth never exist for Me.
Discrimination arises. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Pure," etc. Through the realization "I am Brahman," the scent of conventional duality [is removed].
When, by means of this realization, the scent of duality is eliminated, then there occurs the direct perception of the orb of the innermost inward-shining Sun.

The meaning is that by the practice of that meditation, one who has grasped the path to liberation known as right knowledge— which is characterized by the form of Brahman— becomes fully matured and has accomplished all that was to be done.
An examination of the mind as the cause of bondage and liberation:

The mind, characterized by volition and the like, is the cause of bondage; the mind freed from that becomes the means for liberation. One who possesses such [a mind] is withdrawn from the external manifold of the eyes and other senses.
Free from the scent of conceptual proliferation, seeing the entire world as his own self, having abandoned egoism,
contemplating "I am Brahman," and meditating that "all this is indeed this Self," he becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done. || 6 ||
He states that the mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation, which manifest from the ten stages beginning with one's own ignorance—thus:

"volition and so forth" (verse 5). In this way, the yogi whose inner self is free of volition becomes devoid of the delusion regarding the existence of anything other than himself, and realizes that there is only Brahman, which is without a second.
He says "tadvān" (possessing that) to show that the yogi becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done at the very moment of [that] feeling:

"tadvān" refers to the knower who possesses the non-conceptual state (*nirvikalpa-vṛtti*). By contemplating everything in accordance with the Vedic scripture, "All this is indeed Brahman," through contemplation accompanied by knowledge, [he attains his goal]. || 6 ||
Thus ends the fourth section:
through the practice of non-conceptual samādhi, one attains the state of being a preeminent knower of Brahman;
the yogi becomes the fully perfected Brahman that transcends the fourth state (turiyatita). Him they call "Brahman."
They praise [him] thus: || 1 || He is the worthy recipient of praise from all the world, whose nature is to wander through all worlds;

having cast the drop (*bindu*) into the movement toward the Supreme Self, he proceeds by following the state of unbroken bliss—the yoga-nidra that is pure non-duality, free from dullness, and innate mindlessness.
He becomes liberated while living. || 2 ||

Having become one who has realized Brahman (*brahmabhūta*), he is a yogi whose essence is solely Brahman. To him, the knower of Brahman who possesses such knowledge— [to him] who is distinguished by the aforementioned attributes— the yogi, having cast the drop (*bindu*) into the sky of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and having dissolved the mind into the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), [realizes] the non-dual purity (*śuddhādvaita*) which is the substratum of that dissolution.

In the non-dual Brahman, which is the purification of the support for the dissolution of the mind (*manolaya*), there is the yoga-sleep of innate non-inertness (*ajāḍya-sahajāmanaska-yoganidrā*), which is non-conceptual absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*) due to the absence of states such as inert waking and so forth.
Because one attains (*padyate*) that state through its being unbroken bliss, it is called the "state of unbroken bliss" (*akhaṇḍānanda-pada*); this follows from that [attainment].
The meaning is that by means of uninterrupted continuity, one becomes the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman. || 2 ||
The attainment of Brahman, whose nature is undivided bliss, occurs;
and the yogis become immersed in that ocean of bliss. Compared to that, Indra and the other gods possess only slight bliss. Thus is the supreme yogi who has attained bliss.
"Thus it is; this is the Upaniṣad. || 4 ||
And that Brahman which is renowned as an ocean of waveless bliss—[that too]. || 3 ||
Due to the conceit "I am Indra and so forth," there is a state of limited bliss; by contrast, it is thus [liberated] through the ascent into the state of the unlimited Brahman. 4.
Thus ends the fifth section;
thus ends the second Brāhmaṇa;
[now begins] the third Brāhmaṇa.

Accompanied by the Śāmbhavī-mudrā, the great sage Yājñavalkya questioned the Puruṣa within the maṇḍala: "O Lord, although the characteristics of Amanaska have been described, I have forgotten them; please state those characteristics once again."

"So be it," said the Person of the Maṇḍala. "This is the Amanaska, the supreme secret; by the knowledge of which one attains fulfillment, and which is eternally endowed with the Śāmbhavī Mudrā. || 2 ||

Yājñavalkya asks Āditya about the characteristics of the "mindless" (amanaska) state for the sake of clarifying his dull intellect; thus he says, "Yājñavalkya. Why? [He asks] "O Master," etc. (1). Having accepted that question, the Blessed One gives the answer: "So be it. What?

With the word "that" (tat), he praises the knowledge that is about to be described—referring to it as "this" (idam): that wherein the mind dissolves and attains the state of non-mindfulness; this is [the knowledge] by which the yogi [attains liberation]. || 2 ||
Through the vision of the targets of the cognition of the Supreme Self, one attains the state of Amanaska;

having seen those targets of its cognition through the vision of the Supreme Self, thereafter [one perceives] the Lord of All, the immeasurable, unborn, auspicious, supreme ether, which is without support and non-dual.

Perceiving within his very self the Supreme Brahman— the single goal of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the rest, and the cause of all— and having understood with certainty that this is indeed the dwelling in the cave of the heart,
he transcends the dualities of existence and non-existence; thereafter, he experiences the state of Manonmanī, which is fully realized consciousness.

Through the power of the cessation of all the senses, one attains the Supreme Brahman— immovable like a lamp placed in a windless spot by means of the yoga of the mental flow— which is the ocean of the bliss of Brahmā, the mind-transcending happiness;
this is the fourth state of consciousness (turya-caitanya) realized through the vision of the Supreme Self, perfected by the means of the Śāmbhavī-mudrā.

In the phrase "of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and so forth," the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental; for [the Self] has been carved out by them through the cognition of the identity of the Self with all.
By the word "cave" (guhā), the cave of the intellect (buddhi-guhā) is meant; therein, [He exists] in the form of the inner self (pratyag-rūpa) which illumines its own modifications.

Because of dwelling [therein], it is the "dwelling in the cave" (*guhāviharaṇa*); that state wherein the mind attains the condition of *unmanī* (the state beyond mind), which is freedom from volitional thought (*niḥsaṅkalpatā*), is the experience of "I am Brahman," and this is the experience of *manonmanya*. The remainder is clear and has been explained in various places. || 3 ||
From that comes cessation from saṃsāra; from that, like a withered tree, due to the absence of fainting, sleep, disease, exhalation, and inhalation,
one whose dualities have perished and whose body is forever motionless, having attained supreme peace, [the mind...]
Devoid of movement, it becomes dissolved in the Supreme Self. || 4 ||
It has been stated that the yogi, having thus known his own self, attains the Supreme Brahman. Following that,
raising the doubt as to whether the yogi continues to transmigrate as before,
[the author] says "Then" (tataḥ), explaining that because of the absence of the mind— which sustains the process of transmigration— he becomes Brahman itself.

The dissolution of the vital breaths and the internal organ into a state resembling [the state of] sleep is the meaning of "fainting" (*mūrchā*). Being "composed of that" means being a transformation thereof; like the states of fainting and sleep, because there is an absence of activity such as inhalation, exhalation, desire, and volition, one is "devoid of dualities."
By ceasing all external and internal activities, having embraced supreme tranquility, one becomes Brahman and triumphs;
one comes under the sway of long-lasting, non-conceptual samādhi. At that time, that mind, being empty—
Through the path of the stars (tārakamārga) and by means of the dissolution of the instruments (karaṇavilaya), there occurs the destruction of the mind (manonāśa).

Once the entire aggregate of the senses has perished—like the milk from a cow's udder after the flow of milk has ceased—the destruction of the mind comes to pass; that itself is the state of "no-mind" (amanaska). Following that, one is eternally pure.

Through the instruction "I am indeed the Supreme Self; thou art That" (tattvamasi), one becomes fulfilled and achieves the goal of life, filled with indivisible bliss by means of the Tāraka Yoga path, realizing: "Thou art indeed I, and I am indeed thou. || 6 ||

To the question of how the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*) can occur for a yogin established in *samādhi* while the collection of sense organs (*indriyagrāma*) still exists, he says: "Milk... [and so forth]. That which is said to "become" is precisely that. (5) If, at some time, without attaining dissolution into the formless (*virūpalaya*), the mind reaches dissolution into the formed (*sarūpalaya*) and then emerges outwardly, then—
Thereafter, by means of the path of the conjunction with the Tāraka, the yogi attains the dissolution of the collection of sense organs into their diverse forms.
Then the yogi becomes "unbroken"; the meaning is that he becomes Brahman itself. || 6 ||
Thus ends the first section:
through the attainment of the *unmanī* state, the yogi becomes one with the Self of Brahman; with his mind immersed in the perfectly full supreme space, he has reached the state of *unmanī*.

Having renounced the entire group of sense organs, with the fruit of absolute liberation ripened by the mass of merit accumulated over many births, and with all the impurities of affliction dispelled by unbroken bliss, he becomes one who has accomplished his purpose, realizing: "I am Brahman. || 1 ||
Saying, "I am indeed you; there is no difference because of the fullness of the Supreme Self," he embraced the disciple and led him to pure consciousness.
Furthermore, how does the yogi become one who has accomplished his purpose? To this he says: "Paripūrṇa" (fully perfected).
This means one who has attained the state of *unmanī*, having reached the long-lasting state free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*). || 1 ||

The mantra also reiterates the meaning stated by the Brāhmaṇa: "Thou art indeed [I]. Addressing Yājñavalkya, the Person within the Maṇḍala says: "O Yājñavalkya, because I, the Supreme Self, am of a complete nature, thou art indeed I; there is no difference between us. Thus speaking, he [addresses] his own disciple, Yājñavalkya.
Embracing his own realization intensely, he brought forth the wisdom that "I am indeed Brahman. || 2 ||
Thus ends the second section;
thus ends the third Brāhmaṇa;
[now begins] the fourth Brāhmaṇa.
The knowledge of the fivefold ether and its fruit.
Now, Yājñavalkya questioned the Puruṣa within the Maṇḍala:
"Explain in detail the characteristics of the fivefold ether. He replied: "Space..."

There are five [spaces]: the supreme space (parākāśa), the great space (mahākāśa), the solar space (sūryākāśa), and the ultimate space (paramākāśa). The space consisting of darkness exists both outside and inside;
the supreme space (parākāśa) resembles the fire of cosmic destruction and exists both outside and inside.
The Great Space (mahākāśa) is the reality that resembles immeasurable luster both internally and externally;
the Solar Space (sūryākāśa) resembles the sun both internally and externally; and the Supreme Space (paramākāśa) is the inexpressible light, all-pervading, characterized by unsurpassed bliss. || 3 ||
Thus, by seeing the internal object of focus, one becomes of that same nature. || 4 ||

Furthermore, Yājñavalkya, out of compassion for those of dull intellect, asks about the characteristics of the fivefold ether (*vyomapañcaka*), saying: "Now," etc. Why [does he ask]? [He says: "Ether," etc.
(1). He said: "What is that?"—"Space," etc. (2). In that regard, as to what kind of space it is:
Jaḍabhūti says "sabāhya" (together with the external) [in response to the question] "What is the supreme space (parākāśa)? Here,
Jaḍabhūti, who is the delusion that devours [all things], says "sabāhya" because the space shines forth as being beyond that,
since it pervades the entire mass of insentient matter (jaḍabhūti).
The state of being the supreme space (*parākāśatva*). Regarding the question "What is the great space (*mahākāśa*)?", he says:

"That which possesses the external," etc. This refers to the manifestation of the play of absorption (*grāsalīlābhūti*), which devours the manifestations of insentient matter (*jaḍa*) and delusion (*moha*); for that manifestation of play pervades both the insentient and the delusive, and thus [the great space] is defined in relation to them.
Because it shines forth as the very essence whose nature is immeasurable splendor. To the question "What is the solar space?

he says: "With the external," etc., meaning that it is the eternal manifestation (*nitya-bhūti*) which subsumes the triad of manifestations beginning with the insentient (*jaḍa*). This is because the eternal manifestation shines forth like the sun, which illuminates everything by pervading the triad of manifestations beginning with the play (*līlā*).

As for the question of what the nature of the supreme space (*paramākāśa*) is, it is said to be "indefinable" because it pervades the eternally existing reality (*nityabhūti*) and so forth; this is because it is established through the negation of all elements of duality contained within the fourfold eternally existing reality (*nityādibhūti*) of the three-quarters (*tripādbhūti*).
The meaning is that the status of being qualifiers such as "unsurpassed" and so forth is logically established. || 3 ||
He states the fruit of the knowledge of the five elements consisting of the five voids with the words "evam" (thus). || 4 ||
He who does not correctly understand this— the nine wheels that encompass the essence of all royal yogas, the six supports, the three targets, and the five voids— is merely a yogi in name.
Having embraced the entire essence of the *rājayoga*, he concludes with the words "the nine wheels" (*navacakra*).

The six wheels beginning with the *mūlādhāra* and the three wheels resulting from the division of the palate-space and the brow-wheel—altogether, these constitute the nine wheels. The three targets (*lakṣya*) and the five voids (*vyoma*) have already been explained.

He who does not know all this correctly, due to ignorance of its true nature (*tadyāthātmya*), becomes a "yogi in name only" based merely on his knowledge of the literal meaning of the texts. However, he who knows it as it truly is—that yogi has accomplished what was to be done; such is the meaning. || 5 ||
Thus ends the fourth Brāhmaṇa.
The fifth Brāhmaṇa: The method for the practice of dissolving the mind into the Supreme Self.
The mind with its objects leads to bondage; the mind without its objects leads to liberation. || 1 ||

Therefore, everything is the domain of the mind. That very mind, when it has become supportless and matured in the state of *manonmanī*, becomes fit for dissolution (*laya*). One should practice that dissolution within Me, who am the fullness; for I alone am the cause of the dissolution of the mind.
Of that unstruck sound, there is the resonance;
within the resonance is the light, and within the light is the mind. (4)
That mind which performs the work of creating, maintaining, and destroying the three worlds—that mind dissolves; that is the supreme state of Viṣṇu.

Anticipating the question of what constitutes the cause of bondage and liberation, he states that it is precisely attachment or non-attachment to sense objects—“saviṣayam” (along with objects)—in verse 1. Since this is so, therefore: that very mind which becomes pure through the practice of yoga is itself without support, being free from connection with sense objects—verse 2.

Regarding the question "What is the locus of dissolution?", it is said here: "That is its dissolution" (III). That which is the locus of the dissolution of all things—that very thing, when the particularities residing in the substratum (the container) dependent upon the contained (the superstratum) have ceased, is the non-differentiated supreme state; thus he says: "Of the unstruck" (anāhatasya).

The mind— which is conceptualized as the inner light within the unstruck abode (anāhata-bhavana) and which effects the creation, maintenance, and destruction of that which is other than itself— dissolves therein; that locus of dissolution, from the perspective of ultimate reality, is the state of Viṣṇu, which is without any locus.
The meaning is that it remains. || 4-5 ||
Through the practice of mindlessness (*amanaska*), the attainment of the state of Brahman is achieved;
through absorption in That, pure non-duality (*śuddhādvaita*) is realized due to the absence of differentiation. This alone is the supreme reality.
(6) Such a knower of That should conduct himself among the world with a dull demeanor, like one intoxicated by power or like a ghost. (7)

Thus, by the very practice of non-mentalization (amanaska), there arises eternal contentment, diminished urine and feces, moderation in food, firmness of the limbs, freedom from dullness and sleep, the absence of movement caused by the winds (vāyu), the vision of Brahman, and the attainment of the true nature of bliss known through realization. || 8 ||
Because that mind, which is the cause of duality, has dissolved, there is then no distinction between the inner self and the Supreme;

this is precisely what you asked when you inquired about the supreme reality. He who knows the supreme reality in the manner I have described is a knower of That (taj-jña); he should so conduct himself.
Because there is no purpose in proclaiming one's own greatness. || 7 ||
(300) To the question, "What accomplishment arises from such practice of *amanaska*? he says: "In this way.

When the yogi has ascended to non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) samādhi, then, because no mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*) that cause dissatisfaction arise, there is constant satisfaction. Furthermore, even upon emerging from samādhi, [there is control] over urine, feces, and so forth, by means of simple breath-retention (*kumbhaka*).

Due to the drying up [of fluids], there is a reduction in urine and other secretions; due to the lack of space in the abdomen, there is little food intake. Nevertheless, by the power of yoga, there is firmness of the limbs. Because there is no dullness or sleep at every step, one is "without dullness or sleep," which is non-conceptual samādhi (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*). In that state, because of the absence of movement of the gaze and the vital breath (*prāṇa-vāyu*),...

The perfection (siddhi) arises, which consists in abiding as Brahman alone—the very nature of bliss unknown [to ordinary experience]—because it has become the object of the unwavering vision of Brahman and transcends the range of speech and mind.
The meaning is that the knower remains in that very form. || 8 ||
Such is the greatness of the one who has attained the state of Amanaska;
thus, this Paramahaṃsa Sannyāsī, devoted to drinking the nectar of Brahman produced through long-term Samādhi, becomes an Avadhūta. By the mere sight of him, the entire world becomes purified.
It comes to pass: even one who is ignorant, by being intent on its service, becomes liberated. It delivers one hundred and one members of his lineage.
Furthermore, the group consisting of his mother, father, wife, and children becomes liberated—this is the Upaniṣad. || 9 ||

He who knows thus is indeed the primary Avadhūta; everything that comes within the range of his vision attains a state of total wholeness. By serving him, even an ignorant person is liberated, and his entire lineage attains fulfillment. Thus the scripture concludes with the word "evam" (thus). The term "ity upaniṣat" signifies the end of the teaching.
This marks the conclusion of the present Upaniṣad. || 9 ||
Thus ends the fifth Brāhmaṇa. This commentary on the Maṇḍala-brāhmaṇa, which has Brahman as its subject matter, has been written by Upaniṣad-brahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra.
The treatise known as the Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇavyākhyā is recorded as consisting of three hundred [verses].
Thus ends the commentary on the Maṇḍala Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣad, completing the forty-eighth [treatise] in the illustrious exposition of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the Īśa.
